analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue federal law enforcement agencies for officers' rights violations, even if the officer has immunity.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a Senate hearing, vote, or floor action after being referred to the Judiciary Committee in June 2021, and it died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change a civil rights law so that people who say a federal law enforcement officer violated their constitutional rights could sue the federal agency that employed the officer. The agency would have to pay for the officer's conduct even if the officer personally had immunity from suit. That closes a gap in current law, where victims of federal officer misconduct often cannot recover damages at all.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are harmed by federal law enforcement officers — for example, someone injured or wrongly arrested by a federal agent — would gain a way to be compensated, with the agency rather than the individual officer paying the judgment. Taxpayers would also stop funding the defense of conduct the law says is illegal, since liability would attach to the employer directly.

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives people a statutory right to sue federal law enforcement agencies for officers' constitutional violations, addressing the gap in current law that restricts lawsuits against federal officers in many cases.
It makes the agency liable for an officer's conduct 'regardless of whether the officer has any defense or immunity from suit or liability,' so victims can recover even when the officer is shielded.
It expressly waives sovereign immunity for federal law enforcement agencies for these claims, removing the government's usual shield from being sued.
It does not limit any remedies available against the individual officer, so accountability is added, not shifted away from wrongdoers.

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies would pay judgments for their officers' rights violations, out of federal (taxpayer) funds. Agencies would face pressure to screen and train officers more carefully, and misconduct settlements would become a federal budget cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal law enforcement agencies and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Because liability would fall on the employing agency and be paid with public funds, taxpayers would ultimately cover judgments for officer misconduct, which critics say is a real cost even where it creates correct incentives.

Holding agencies liable without requiring proof of a policy or custom removes a traditional safeguard, and defenders of qualified immunity argue immunity protects officers who must make split-second decisions in good faith; the bill would bypass that defense for the employer side.

Opponents of expanded police-liability legislation generally argued such measures would make recruitment and aggressive lawful policing harder; that objection was not resolved in this Congress because the bill never advanced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people whose rights are violated by federal officers, the benefit is substantial: today many have no practical way to recover damages, and this bill would give them a direct claim against the employer with a guaranteed waiver of immunity. The main cost is that judgments would be paid with public money, which is the intended design — agencies are supposed to internalize the price of misconduct — but it does mean taxpayers fund the remedy rather than individual officers. On balance it is a well-aimed fix to a specific, documented gap in the law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which took no further action on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Padilla introduced the bill on June 17, 2021; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
Eight senators — 7 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents — cosponsored the bill.
No further action was taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and the bill never left the Judiciary Committee before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement agencies and officers keep the practical shield from lawsuits, and victims of federal officer misconduct remain without the remedy this bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal law enforcement agencies and officers

for.name: Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the Senate floor at introduction.

for.name: 7 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Dick Durbin, D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 17, 2021 and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all recorded support came from Democrats and independents, with no Republican cosponsors, so the partisan shape of opposition is unknown from the record.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies (e.g., federal police and investigative services)
industries.note: The bill would strip away the practical shield that lets agencies and their officers avoid paying for constitutional violations, making them directly liable and waiving sovereign immunity. Their interest in the status quo runs against victims seeking redress.

industries.industry: Government legal defense establishment (Justice Department litigators and outside counsel defending federal officers)
industries.note: Fewer immunity defenses and direct employer liability would shrink the volume of officer-side defense litigation and make claims easier to resolve against the government.
